title: Optometry Eye Clinic Scope Tasks: Nightly vs. Periodic Duty Roster for Optometry & Optical Retail Offices
seoTitle: Optometry Eye Clinic Scope Tasks: Nightly vs Periodic Duty Roster
metaDescription: Optometry eye clinic scope tasks by zone: nightly, weekly and quarterly duties, minutes per task, and specialty labor at $55-$95/hr. Price it in our tool.
excerpt: An optometry office needs a duty roster that covers boutique-grade glass in the showroom, disinfected chairs in exam lanes, and careful dusting around delicate instruments. This guide lays out nightly versus periodic tasks and shows which ones drive labor above standard office rates.
quickAnswer: An optometry scope should assign nightly glass and mirror polishing in the optical showroom, disinfection of exam chairs, armrests, and pretest counters, full restroom sanitation, and vacuuming plus damp mopping. Weekly and quarterly duties, such as frame-board dusting, baseboards, LVT machine scrubbing, and carpet extraction, add labor billed at $35-$65 per hour standard or $55-$95 per hour for specialty work.

blocks.text: Building the roster around three optometry zones

The fastest way to get comparable bids for an eye care practice is to hand every vendor the same roster, organized by zone and frequency. Optometry offices split naturally into the optical showroom, the clinical corridor of pretest rooms and exam lanes, and back-of-house space such as the edging lab, contact lens storage, and staff breakroom. Each zone has a different soil profile. The showroom collects fingerprints and lint, exam lanes collect skin oils on chair arms and chin rests, and the lab collects lens dust and polishing compound residue.

Clear boundaries matter more here than in most offices. Instruments such as phoropters, slit lamps, and autorefractors are expensive and fragile, so the roster must say exactly what cleaners touch and what they leave for clinical staff. Most disputes between practices and vendors trace back to a vague line like 'dust exam rooms' that left a new night cleaner wiping a phoropter lens with a damp rag.
The nightly roster below assumes a 3,000 sq ft two-doctor practice with an optical showroom, two pretest rooms, three exam lanes, a contact lens training station, and two restrooms.

blocks.caption: Nightly optometry scope tasks with typical minutes per visit
rows: Polish display case tops, mirrors, dispensing tables, and storefront glass
Vacuum carpet tile aisles, detail around frame towers
Disinfect exam chair upholstery, armrests, and counters; empty trash; damp mop
Wipe counters and patient stools; dust floor around instrument tables without touching optics
Clean and disinfect sink, mirror, counter, and soap dispenser
Disinfect chair arms, check-in counter, pens, door levers; vacuum
Full fixture disinfection, mirror, restock, mop
Empty trash, sweep lab floor, wipe breakroom counters and sink

blocks.text: That totals 102 to 146 minutes per visit, or about 1.7 to 2.4 crew hours. Roughly 35 to 51 minutes fall into the specialty column, mostly glass polishing and exam chair disinfection, which is why optometry offices land above plain office pricing even at similar square footage.

blocks.title: Hands off the optics
blocks.text: Write a no-touch rule for phoropters, slit lamp oculars, tonometer tips, retinal cameras, and lensmeters. Cleaners may dust instrument tables and stands only after clinical staff cover or park the instruments. One scratched objective lens can cost more than a year of janitorial service.

items: Dust frame boards and shelving edges with a dry microfiber cloth, working top to bottom so lens dust does not resettle on cleaned glass.
Detail all interior glass partitions and the frame-styling mirrors with a 14-inch solid brass Ettore squeegee and replaceable pro rubber for streak-free results that cloths alone cannot match.
Scrub the contact lens training sink, breakroom sink, and restroom porcelain with non-rusting 3M Scotch-Brite heavy-duty pads that will not scratch fixtures.
Wipe baseboards, door frames, and kick plates throughout the clinical corridor.
Flat-mop all LVT or VCT with a Rubbermaid HYGEN 18-inch microfiber kit; its onboard reservoir eliminates dirty-bucket water in tight exam lanes.
Clean inside trash receptacles and wipe light switches and thermostats.
Dust vents, return grilles, and the top edges of wall-mounted acuity monitors.

blocks.text: Weekly duties typically add 60 to 80 minutes. On a three-times-weekly contract, that is about 4.3 to 5.8 extra crew hours per month using 4.333 weeks per month. At standard rates of $35-$65 per hour, budget roughly $150-$375 per month, and confirm the vendor's proposal shows these tasks explicitly.

blocks.caption: Periodic optometry office tasks and typical billing
rows: Machine scrub and burnish LVT or VCT in lanes and lab
Hot-water extraction of showroom and waiting carpet
$0.03-$0.06 per sq ft per month amortized
High dusting of track lighting over frame boards

blocks.text: For a 3,000 sq ft office, amortized deep floor care at $0.03-$0.06 per sq ft per month is $90-$180, which smooths seasonal spikes after winter salt or summer storms and keeps the showroom carpet from matting in the frame-selection aisles.
Which tasks push labor above standard office rates

Three categories drive specialty pricing in eye care. First, display glass and mirrors in the optical showroom, where customers judge the practice by streaks they see while trying on frames. Second, disinfection of exam chairs and pretest surfaces to the full EPA label contact time. Third, careful work around instruments, which slows the crew because cleaners must dust around fragile equipment rather than across it. On the nightly roster, those categories add 35 to 51 specialty minutes per visit; across 13 visits per month that is 7.6 to 11 hours, or about $418-$1,045 per month at $55-$95 per hour.

items.name: Map rooms to zones
items.text: Label each room showroom, clinical, or back-of-house on a floor plan you share with every bidder.

items.name: Set task frequencies
items.text: Assign each task nightly, weekly, monthly, or quarterly so bids rest on identical assumptions.

items.name: Write the instrument rule
items.text: State which surfaces cleaners may touch in exam lanes and pretest rooms, and who covers equipment at close.

items.name: Request split labor hours
items.text: Ask vendors to show standard and specialty hours separately to confirm glass and lane work were priced.

items.name: Inspect monthly
items.text: Walk the showroom under display lighting and score glass, then check chair arms and floors in each lane.

blocks.title: Close-of-day handoff
blocks.text: Have the last optician on duty park instruments, cover slit lamps, lock frame cases, and clear dispensing tables before the crew arrives. A two-minute handoff saves ten minutes of crew time and removes the main risk of equipment damage.

faqs.q: How long does a nightly clean take in a 3,000 sq ft optometry office?
faqs.a: About 1.7 to 2.4 crew hours for a practice with three exam lanes, two pretest rooms, an optical showroom, and two restrooms. Weekly detail adds 60 to 80 minutes per week. On a three-times-weekly schedule, multiplied by 4.333 weeks, expect roughly 27 to 37 labor hours per month before periodic floor care.

faqs.q: Who cleans exam chairs and chin rests in an eye clinic?
faqs.a: Clinical staff should wipe chin rests, forehead bars, and frequently touched instrument handles between patients using the disinfectant the instrument manufacturer approves. The janitorial crew handles nightly disinfection of chair upholstery, armrests, counters, and floors. Splitting the duties in writing prevents gaps and protects delicate optics.

faqs.q: What chemicals belong in an optometry cleaning scope?
faqs.a: List an EPA-registered disinfectant for restrooms and exam chair upholstery, an ammonia-free glass cleaner safe for coated mirrors and display glass, and a neutral floor cleaner. Require Safety Data Sheets on site under OSHA HazCom. Many practices choose Green Seal or Safer Choice products for the showroom to avoid odors while customers are trying on frames.

faqs.q: Is inside-display-case cleaning part of nightly service?
faqs.a: Usually not. Locked cases hold frame inventory, so inside cleaning is typically monthly and requires staff to unlock and supervise. Nightly service covers case tops and exterior glass. Price inside-case cleaning as a periodic line item so it does not become an unpaid expectation.

faqs.q: What should be excluded from an optometry janitorial scope?
faqs.a: Common exclusions include cleaning or disinfecting ophthalmic instruments, handling lens edging equipment or coolant, removing biohazard or sharps waste, laundering, exterior storefront windows above reach, and moving frame inventory. Listing exclusions keeps bids comparable and defines liability if something is damaged.
